title: One programmable repair for many photoreceptor and RPE gene defects

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reusable system for repairing different inherited genetic defects in surviving photoreceptors—the retinal cells that detect light—or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which supports them. The delivery system and editing machinery would remain substantially the same across diseases, while a guide or repair template would change to direct treatment to a different genetic target. The intended result is preservation of native visual function through repair at the affected gene.

Conceptual synthesis: the defining advance is demonstrated reuse across unrelated genetic defects. Sharing some delivery technology among separate gene-specific treatments would not by itself establish this capability. The platform would need to accommodate meaningful differences among targets while retaining a common delivery and editing architecture; the exact boundary of what may change must be defined before testing.

The rationale is a broad and heterogeneous genetic landscape. Vanzara and colleagues reported 313 genes in a curated RetNet list using the resource accessed on 8 December 2024. Their comparison also found differences in coverage among gene lists, so this figure describes a particular curated dataset rather than a universal or permanently current total of retinal disease genes.

significance.text: Conditional significance: if one platform safely produced durable functional benefit across unrelated retinal genotypes, it would establish reusable native-gene repair across multiple inherited retinal diseases. The direct consequence would be preservation of visual function in the successfully treated eyes and genotypes. Applying one technological principle across this diverse genetic landscape could be substantially more consequential than another isolated gene-specific success, but testing several genotypes would not establish coverage of the entire disease class.

Conditional downstream possibilities include extending treatment to additional rare genotypes and reducing how much delivery and editing development must be repeated for each target. Those benefits would depend on how consistently the platform transfers between genes, mutation mechanisms and retinal cell types. A common platform would still require target-specific evidence of efficacy and safety; it would not automatically make every inherited retinal disorder treatable.

The intended benefit concerns cells that remain alive and functionally recoverable. Repairing their genetic defect does not itself demonstrate replacement of lost photoreceptors, reconstruction of RPE or recovery of missing tissue connections. NEI's 2021 strategic plan treats cell replacement and ocular gene editing as related regenerative research directions, supporting this distinction without establishing that every end-stage eye necessarily requires the same intervention.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability, as defined by this proposal, is a common delivery and editing system that can be redirected across unrelated photoreceptor and RPE defects while preserving clinically useful native vision. NEI's November 2021 strategic plan identified optimization of gene delivery and validated clinical outcome measures as gaps in gene-based therapies and prioritized ocular gene editing. These documented priorities ground the proposal, but they do not establish which barriers remain unsolved in November 2026.

Engineering synthesis: the platform would need to deliver effective editing machinery to enough of the intended retinal cells, produce the required correction, and preserve those cells and their function. Retargeting would have to retain acceptable editing accuracy, delivery performance and immune safety. Packaging and payload demands may constrain the architecture, but the supplied review does not verify a specific vector cargo limit, so no numerical limit is asserted.

Mechanism-specific synthesis: dominant inheritance does not imply one universal treatment requirement. For a harmful gain-of-function or dominant-negative allele, adding a normal copy may leave the harmful activity intact, making selective suppression or correction relevant. Other mechanisms require different reasoning. A platform claiming broad reuse must therefore demonstrate that it can handle distinct disease mechanisms, rather than assume all dominant alleles require the same intervention. The supplied retained sources do not verify the original categorical assertion about dominant alleles.

The original research also identifies fragile foveal cones and inefficient delivery into those cells as concerns. These remain candidate technical barriers rather than verified findings in the supplied review, because the retained sources do not establish their extent or present status. The cited October 2025 review was described as discussing narrow gene- or variant-specific indications and vector limitations, but its text was not captured. That access gap limits assessment of the specific claims without showing that they are false.

current_state.text: The Eye article published on 28 January 2025 provides the clearest supported quantitative baseline in the supplied review. Vanzara and colleagues reported 313 RetNet genes after exclusions and gene-symbol curation, using RetNet accessed on 8 December 2024. Their exclusions included duplicate or alternative symbols, mitochondrial genes and loci without identified causative genes. The review reports that the complete two-page article was retained, with no extraction limitation affecting this finding. The count establishes substantial genetic breadth, not 313 interchangeable therapeutic targets or a current total as of November 2026.

The supplied research attributes to an October 2025 Regenerative Medicine review the statement that voretigene neparvovec, marketed as Luxturna, remained the approved gene-addition therapy for RPE65 disease and that no other inherited retinal disease gene therapy had received regulatory approval at that time. It also uses voretigene as a precedent for improved vision in biallelic RPE65 disease. No text from that review was retained, and the clinical precedent was not independently verified in the supplied review. These therefore remain attributed historical claims, not a verified approval inventory or confirmed clinical baseline for November 2026.

The supplied research reports that EDIT-101 targeted one deep-intronic CEP290 variant and treated 14 people, citing a New England Journal of Medicine paper dated 6 May 2024. It reports a mean visual-acuity change of −0.21 logMAR, four participants reaching a 0.3 logMAR gain, and no treatment-related serious adverse events. The paper was not captured, so the supplied review could not inspect the sample size, endpoint definitions, analysis population, follow-up or safety findings. These numbers are preserved as unverified reports rather than accepted or rejected results. Even if confirmed, a study of one variant would demonstrate a narrower capability than reuse across unrelated genotypes, and its reported safety outcome would not establish absence of all risks.

NEI's November 2021 strategic plan documented goals for gene delivery, clinical measurement and ocular gene editing. It also presented cell-specific control of gene expression enabling vision restoration as an aspirational prediction. The supplied review retained the full 19-page executive summary and identified that prediction in its aspirational section. This is evidence of a historical research ambition, not a demonstration of restoration or of the proposed reusable repair platform.

Evidence boundary: the supplied materials do not establish that clinical retinal editing has been limited exclusively to one variant, nor do they establish whether a reusable repair platform remains undemonstrated as of 1 November 2026. The freshness search record is empty. The retained sources also do not substantiate the original characterization of optogenetics and neurotrophic factors as substituting for lost cells. Those approaches should not be grouped under that mechanism without further evidence; neither is shown here to constitute native-gene repair.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: one delivery and editing platform, changed only by its guide or repair template, should produce durable, clinically meaningful preservation of visual acuity or retinal sensitivity across several unrelated genotypes. The test set should include a large-gene challenge and a dominant allele selected to test a specified disease mechanism. Follow-up should extend over years. A single-gene phase 1 success would not satisfy this proposed definition of reuse. These are proposed criteria, not published consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed operational definitions: studies should prespecify what qualifies as a large gene, an unchanged platform, clinically meaningful preservation, sufficient durability and acceptable safety. For the large-gene case, the study should explain which delivery or repair constraint the target actually tests. Platform sameness should specify which delivery components, editor, route and manufacturing elements remain fixed; any target-specific changes should be disclosed. No separate vector program for each gene should be needed to satisfy the strict version of this proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed operational definitions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing evidence should connect molecular repair with sustained visual function and distinguish treatment effects from measurement variability and expected disease progression through an appropriate comparison. Safety assessment should address unintended editing, inflammation, immune effects, tissue injury and loss of remaining vision. Acceptable immune safety need not mean complete absence of any immune response. These requirements extend NEI's documented emphasis on delivery and validated clinical measurements, but the exact thresholds remain to be designed.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: results should be reproducible in independent cohorts and, where feasible, independent centers, with transparent reporting of target-specific failures and changes to the platform. Studies should define the required surviving cell population, eligible disease stages and which photoreceptor or RPE populations were reached. Success would establish breadth across the tested settings; no finite set of genotypes could prove literal universality, efficacy after extensive cell loss or transferability to every retinal disorder.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OPH-02, Biological reconstruction of foveal cones, RPE, and their blood supply, has the closest anatomical overlap. OPH-07 aims to repair genetic defects in surviving cells, whereas OPH-02 concerns rebuilding the cells and supporting tissue. They could be complementary where genetic correction and tissue reconstruction are both needed. OPH-08, Reperfusion of established retinal capillary dropout, addresses retinal circulation rather than genetic repair. These distinctions use the supplied roster titles; full records for those concepts were not provided.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-01, Retinotopic reconnection of retinal ganglion cell axons to brain targets, addresses transmission from the retina to the brain. OPH-05, Patterned vision from the brain when the eye cannot send signals, addresses a route to vision that bypasses failed ocular signaling. OPH-09, Reopening of the human visual critical period, concerns visual-system plasticity. None is interchangeable with repairing photoreceptor or RPE genes, and success in OPH-07 would not itself establish reconnection, a brain-based visual interface or renewed plasticity.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-10, Arrest of glaucomatous ganglion-cell death when pressure is not the lever, shares the goal of preserving retinal neurons but targets ganglion-cell survival in glaucoma. OPH-11, Prevention of progression from early or intermediate AMD to late AMD, shares an interest in preventing retinal degeneration and may overlap anatomically at photoreceptors and RPE. Its disease-level prevention goal is distinct from demonstrated reuse of locus-specific repair across inherited genotypes.

Roster-based synthesis: OPH-03, Reversal of established cataract without removing the lens, and OPH-04, A manufactured cornea that clears vascularized stromal opacity, address optical structures in front of the retina. OPH-06, A closed-loop control that sets axial eye growth, concerns regulation of eye growth. These entries address different causes of visual impairment; none is subsumed by a retinal gene-repair platform.

change_log.change: Preserved OPH-07's identity as a proposed reusable repair platform and clarified the distinction between guide/template retargeting and separate gene-specific programs.
change_log.reason: The defining capability is cross-target reuse; neither a shared delivery component nor a single-gene success establishes it.

change_log.change: Recast the 313-gene figure as a dated, curated RetNet result and incorporated the exclusions and differences among gene lists.
change_log.reason: The retained Eye article supports that specific dataset, not a universal current gene total or a count of interchangeable therapeutic targets.

change_log.change: Retained the reported EDIT-101 numbers, Luxturna approval claim and clinical precedent with explicit attribution and evidence limitations.
change_log.reason: The relevant source texts were not captured. This prevents verification but does not justify discarding the claims as false.

change_log.change: Qualified dominant-allele requirements by disease mechanism and preserved foveal delivery concerns as unverified candidate barriers.
change_log.reason: Dominant inheritance alone does not dictate one treatment strategy, and the supplied retained sources do not substantiate the specific foveal claims.

change_log.change: Removed the collective characterization of optogenetics and neurotrophic factors as substitutes for lost cells.
change_log.reason: The review identified no retained evidence for that grouping, and the claimed mechanism needs separate justification.

change_log.change: Separated NEI's historical priorities and aspirational prediction from demonstrated outcomes and present-day platform availability.
change_log.reason: A strategic research goal cannot establish achievement or continued absence of the capability in 2026.

change_log.change: Limited direct impact to demonstrated genotypes and surviving cells while retaining conditional possibilities for broader reuse.
change_log.reason: Several successful targets would not prove disease-class coverage, and genetic repair alone does not demonstrate reconstruction after cell loss.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria with operational definitions, safety, reproducibility and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: The original proposal needs assessable definitions of benefit, durability, large-gene challenge and platform sameness without presenting them as consensus standards.

change_log.change: Compared OPH-07 with every other supplied roster entry, including OPH-02.
change_log.reason: The roster supplies identities and titles sufficient for bounded conceptual comparisons, although full related records were not provided.

unresolved_issues: The October 2025 review and EDIT-101 paper have no retained text. Their attributed approval, clinical, numerical and safety claims remain unverified.
No freshness search record establishes the clinical landscape or availability of reusable retinal repair as of 1 November 2026.
The extent of foveal cone vulnerability, delivery limitations and clinical editing breadth remains unresolved in the supplied evidence.
The platform architecture, permitted target-specific changes, quantitative benefit and safety thresholds, follow-up duration and definition of a large-gene challenge remain unspecified.
Full related-concept records were not supplied, so overlap and distinctions are limited to the roster titles and OPH-07's stated scope.

The review's recommendation to omit unverified clinical details was not adopted in full: the original quantitative and historical reports are retained with explicit qualifications to preserve useful research detail without treating missing evidence as disproof.
